title: Section 1.0 Board Work #8: Complex Fractions (Fractions within Fractions)
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 02 • Section 1.0 Board Work #8 (Workbook p. 4)
detail: Lecture 02: Fractions, Signed Numbers & Order of Operations
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Board Work #8 (Workbook p. 4):** Simplify each expression into a single fraction or integer value:

$$\mathbf{\dfrac{\ \dfrac{5}{8}\ }{\dfrac{3}{4}}}$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Step 1: } & \text{Interpret the main horizontal fraction bar as a division symbol:} \\
& \dfrac{\ \dfrac{5}{8}\ }{\dfrac{3}{4}} = \dfrac{5}{8} \div \dfrac{3}{4} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 2: } & \text{Apply Keep-Change-Flip (multiply by the reciprocal of the denominator):} \\
& \dfrac{5}{8} \div \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{5}{8} \cdot \dfrac{4}{3} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 3: } & \text{Cross-cancel the common factor of } 4 \text{ between } 4 \text{ and } 8 \text{ before multiplying:} \\
& \dfrac{5}{8 \div 4} \cdot \dfrac{4 \div 4}{3} = \dfrac{5}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{3} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 4: } & \text{Multiply straight across:} \\
& \dfrac{5 \cdot 1}{2 \cdot 3} = \mathbf{\dfrac{5}{6}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall:
**CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: Don't Flip the Top Fraction!**
- Always KEEP the numerator fraction $\frac{5}{8}$ and FLIP the denominator fraction $\frac{3}{4} \to \frac{4}{3}$.
- A complex fraction $\dfrac{A/B}{C/D}$ is mathematically identical to $\dfrac{A}{B} \cdot \dfrac{D}{C}$.
script:
[Prof. Park] Look at Board Work #8 on workbook page 4: simplifying a complex fraction with five-eighths on top and three-fourths on the bottom. Sora, why do multi-tier fractions intimidate students?

[TA Sora] Because students see four numbers stacked vertically and freeze! But remember our core rule: that main middle horizontal bar is simply a division symbol! This is just five-eighths divided by three-fourths!

[Prof. Park] Exactly! A complex fraction is nothing more than division written vertically: $\frac{5}{8} \div \frac{3}{4}$. And what is our golden rule for dividing fractions?

[TA Sora] Keep-Change-Flip! Keep the top fraction, five-eighths, exactly as it is. Change division to multiplication, and flip the bottom fraction, three-fourths, into four-thirds!

[Prof. Park] Now we have five-eighths times four-thirds: $\frac{5}{8} \times \frac{4}{3}$. Before multiplying straight across into twenty over twenty-four, what is your pro-tip, Sora?

[TA Sora] Always cross-cancel first! Notice the diagonal pair: 4 in the numerator and 8 in the denominator divide evenly by 4! That leaves 1 on top and 2 on the bottom.

[Prof. Park] Excellent. Now we simply multiply the surviving factors straight across: five times one gives five on top, and two times three gives six on the bottom!

[TA Sora] Leaving us with five-sixths: $\frac{5}{6}$! That four-story fraction collapsed into a clean, fully reduced five-sixths. Remember: keep the top, flip the bottom, and cross-cancel!

[Prof. Park] Beautifully executed. Let's move on to Board Work #9 on Slide 3!

title: Section 1.0 Board Work #9: Mixed Integer and Fraction Operations
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 02 • Section 1.0 Board Work #9 (Workbook p. 4)
detail: Lecture 02: Fractions, Signed Numbers & Order of Operations
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Board Work #9 (Workbook p. 4):** Simplify each expression into a single fraction or integer value:

$$\mathbf{16 - \dfrac{3}{4} + 9}$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Method 1: } & \text{Group whole numbers first using the Commutative Property:} \\
& (16 + 9) - \dfrac{3}{4} = 25 - \dfrac{3}{4} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 2: } & \text{Convert the whole integer } 25 \text{ to a fraction with denominator 4:} \\
& 25 = \dfrac{25 \cdot 4}{4} = \dfrac{100}{4} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 3: } & \text{Subtract the numerators:} \\
& \dfrac{100}{4} - \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{100 - 3}{4} = \mathbf{\dfrac{97}{4}} \quad \left(\text{or mixed number } 24\dfrac{1}{4}\right)
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Sora's Pro-Tip:** Combining whole numbers first ($16 + 9 = 25$) saves you from finding common denominators across three separate numbers! Work smarter, not harder!
script:
[Prof. Park] On Slide 3, Board Work #9 tests mixed operations combining whole numbers with fractions: evaluate 16 minus three-fourths plus 9. Sora, what strategy keeps this fast and mistake-free?

[TA Sora] Many students immediately convert all three numbers into fourths with a common denominator. That works, but it's unnecessary heavy lifting! Look at the two whole numbers: positive 16 and positive 9!

[Prof. Park] That's the beauty of the Commutative Property! We can group the whole integers first: 16 plus 9 equals 25. Now the problem becomes simply 25 minus three-fourths.

[TA Sora] Much cleaner! How do we subtract three-fourths from 25, Professor?

[Prof. Park] Convert 25 into fourths: 25 times 4 is 100, so 25 is 100 fourths: $\frac{100}{4}$. Now subtract the numerators: 100 minus 3 is 97!

[TA Sora] Giving us the exact improper fraction: 97 over 4! Or as a mixed number, 24 and one-fourth.

[Prof. Park] Grouping integers first saved us from finding large common denominators. Work smarter, not harder!

[TA Sora] Exactly, Professor! On to Board Work #10!

title: Section 1.0 Board Work #10: Simplifying via Prime Factorization
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 02 • Section 1.0 Board Work #10 (Workbook p. 4)
detail: Lecture 02: Fractions, Signed Numbers & Order of Operations
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Board Work #10 (Workbook p. 4):** Simplify each expression into a single fraction or integer value:

$$\mathbf{\dfrac{(16)(3)}{(9)(4)}}$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Foundational Rule: } & \mathbf{\text{Prime Factorization First, Then Cancel!}} \\[0.5em]
\text{Step 1: } & \text{Decompose all composite numbers into their prime factors:} \\
& 16 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2, \quad 9 = 3 \cdot 3, \quad 4 = 2 \cdot 2 \\[0.5em]
\text{Step 2: } & \text{Substitute primes into the numerator and denominator:} \\
& \dfrac{(16)(3)}{(9)(4)} = \dfrac{(2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2) \cdot 3}{(3 \cdot 3) \cdot (2 \cdot 2)} = \dfrac{2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3}{3 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 2} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 3: } & \text{Cancel identical prime factor pairs } \left(\dfrac{2}{2} = 1, \; \dfrac{3}{3} = 1\right): \\
& \dfrac{\cancel{2} \cdot \cancel{2} \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot \cancel{3}}{\cancel{3} \cdot 3 \cdot \cancel{2} \cdot \cancel{2}} = \dfrac{2 \cdot 2}{3} \\[0.8em]
\text{Result: } & \mathbf{\dfrac{4}{3}} \quad \left(\text{or mixed number } 1\dfrac{1}{3}\right)
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall:
**WHY PRIME FACTORIZATION IS OUR GOLDEN PRINCIPLE:**
- **No Guessing Greatest Common Divisors:** Students often struggle to spot that $48$ and $36$ share $12$.
- **Completely Transparent Canceling:** Writing numbers in prime building blocks ($2, 3, 5\dots$) makes matching pairs visible at a glance.
- **Zero Multiplication Traps:** Multiplying first into large numbers like $\frac{48}{36}$ invites arithmetic mistakes; prime factoring first guarantees the fully reduced answer every single time!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 4 brings us to Board Work #10 on workbook page 4: simplify the expression 16 times 3 in the numerator over 9 times 4 in the denominator.

[TA Sora] Professor, when students see this, their natural urge is often to multiply first: 16 times 3 is 48, and 9 times 4 is 36. But then they have to spend time searching for greatest common divisors to reduce 48 over 36!

[Prof. Park] That creates so much stress, especially for students returning to math after a long break! That is why at Gallatin College in M090, our core principle is Prime Factorization first, then cancel!

[TA Sora] Prime factorization eliminates all guesswork! Instead of multiplying into big numbers, we break every single composite number down into its prime building blocks!

[Prof. Park] Exactly. In the numerator, 16 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 2. And 3 is already prime! In the denominator, 9 is 3 times 3, and 4 is 2 times 2.

[TA Sora] Let's write the entire fraction in prime factors: the numerator is 2 times 2 times 2 times 2 times 3, and the denominator is 3 times 3 times 2 times 2!

[Prof. Park] Now look at how clean the canceling is: two 2s in the numerator cancel with two 2s in the denominator, because 2 over 2 is 1! And one 3 on top cancels with one 3 on the bottom!

[TA Sora] What survives? In the numerator, 2 times 2 equals 4. In the denominator, a single 3 remains! That gives us our final answer: four-thirds, or 1 and one-third!

[Prof. Park] No large products, no tricky factoring. Prime factorization makes simplifying fractions completely transparent and foolproof!

[TA Sora] Master this prime factorization habit, and fraction reduction will never trip you up again. Now let's explore division by zero on Slide 5!

title: Section 1.0 Board Work #11 & #12: Division by Zero (Undefined vs. Zero)
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 02 • Section 1.0 Board Work #11 & #12 (Workbook p. 4)
detail: Lecture 02: Fractions, Signed Numbers & Order of Operations
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Board Work #11 & #12 (Workbook p. 4):** Compare the two division expressions:

$$\mathbf{\dfrac{16}{0} \qquad \text{vs.} \qquad \dfrac{0}{16}}$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Problem \#11: } & \dfrac{16}{0} = \mathbf{\text{UNDEFINED}} \\[0.5em]
& \text{Reasoning: Division asks } 0 \cdot (?) = 16. \\
& \text{There is NO real number that multiplied by } 0 \text{ yields } 16! \\[1em]
\text{Problem \#12: } & \dfrac{0}{16} = \mathbf{0} \\[0.5em]
& \text{Reasoning: Division asks } 16 \cdot (?) = 0. \\
& \text{The unique solution is } 0, \text{ since } 16 \cdot 0 = 0.
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall:
**Sora's Famous Mnemonic:**
- $\dfrac{\mathbf{N}}{\mathbf{O}} = \dfrac{\text{Number}}{0} \implies \mathbf{\text{NO! (Undefined - Division by zero is impossible!)}}$
- $\dfrac{\mathbf{O}}{\mathbf{K}} = \dfrac{0}{\text{Number}} \implies \mathbf{\text{OK! (Equals 0)}}$
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 5 features Board Work #11 and #12, comparing 16 over zero versus zero over 16. Sora, why does this distinction trip up so many students on Exam 1?

[TA Sora] Because both expressions use 16 and zero! But the position of zero is everything. Let's look at Board Work #11 first: 16 divided by zero, where zero is in the denominator.

[Prof. Park] In 16 over zero, the result is UNDEFINED! Division asks: what number times zero gives 16? There is no real number that can satisfy that, because zero times anything is always zero! Dividing by zero is completely forbidden in arithmetic.

[TA Sora] Exactly! But now look at Board Work #12: zero divided by 16. Zero is in the numerator!

[Prof. Park] And that equals zero! If you have zero dollars and divide it among 16 friends, each friend gets zero dollars. It is completely defined and equals zero.

[TA Sora] Remember my golden memory trick: OK versus NO! Zero Over K is OK, which equals 0. Number Over Zero spells NO, which is Undefined!

[Prof. Park] Zero on top is fine; zero on the bottom is an absolute barrier!

title: Section 1.0 Board Work #13: PEMDAS Left-to-Right (Division vs. Multiplication)
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 02 • Section 1.0 Board Work #13 (Workbook p. 4)
detail: Lecture 02: Fractions, Signed Numbers & Order of Operations
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Board Work #13 (Workbook p. 4):** Simplify into a single integer value:

$$\mathbf{24 \div 4 \cdot 2}$$
pitfall:
**THE #1 DEADLIEST PEMDAS TRAP:**
- Multiplying first: $4 \cdot 2 = 8$, then $24 \div 8 = 3 \implies \mathbf{\text{WRONG!}}$
- In "PEMDAS", M does NOT precede D! They are a tied pair evaluated from left to right!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 6 brings us to Board Work #13: evaluate 24 divided by 4 times 2. Sora, this is the classic viral internet math trap!

[TA Sora] Absolutely! Millions of people argue over this online because they memorize PEMDAS blindly: 'M comes before D, so multiplication must go first! 4 times 2 is 8, and 24 divided by 8 is 3!'

[Prof. Park] And that answer of 3 is 100% incorrect! Why, Sora?

[TA Sora] Because Multiplication and Division have EQUAL priority! In PEMDAS, they form a tied tier. You must solve them strictly from left to right as they appear!

[Prof. Park] Exactly! Reading left to right: first we encounter 24 divided by 4, which equals 6. Then we multiply that 6 by 2!

[TA Sora] 6 times 2 equals 12! The true, mathematically rigorous answer is 12, not 3!

[Prof. Park] Division was on the left, so division takes priority. Strict left-to-right execution is non-negotiable!

[TA Sora] Let's see the addition and subtraction equivalent on Slide 7!

title: Section 1.0 Board Work #14: PEMDAS Left-to-Right (Subtraction vs. Addition)
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 02 • Section 1.0 Board Work #14 (Workbook p. 4)
detail: Lecture 02: Fractions, Signed Numbers & Order of Operations
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Board Work #14 (Workbook p. 4):** Simplify into a single integer value:

$$\mathbf{17 - 5 + 8}$$
pitfall:
**THE ADDITION TRAP:**
- Adding first: $5 + 8 = 13$, then $17 - 13 = 4 \implies \mathbf{\text{WRONG!}}$
- Addition does NOT take precedence over subtraction! Move strictly left to right: $17 - 5 = 12$, then $12 + 8 = 20$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 7 tests the sibling rule with Board Work #14: evaluate 17 minus 5 plus 8. Sora, what trap awaits here?

[TA Sora] The exact same trap! Students think 'A comes before S in PEMDAS, so I must add 5 plus 8 first to get 13, and then 17 minus 13 equals 4!'

[Prof. Park] And once again, that answer of 4 is completely incorrect! Why?

[TA Sora] Because Addition and Subtraction share EQUAL priority! Just like multiplication and division, they are solved strictly from left to right!

[Prof. Park] Working left to right: first we calculate 17 minus 5, which gives 12. Then we take 12 and add 8!

[TA Sora] 12 plus 8 equals 20! Think of your bank account: you have $17, spend $5 at the store leaving $12, then deposit an $8 check. You have $20, not $4!

[Prof. Park] Real-world accounting and algebra follow the exact same rule: evaluate chronologically from left to right!

[TA Sora] Now let's master the exponent sign trap on Slide 8!

title: Section 1.0 Exponent Pitfall: Base Identification in Signed Powers
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 02 • Section 1.0 Arithmetic Traps (Workbook p. 4)
detail: Lecture 02: Fractions, Signed Numbers & Order of Operations
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Section 1.0 Exponent Pitfall:** Contrast the base of each power:

$$\mathbf{(-3)^2 \qquad \text{vs.} \qquad -3^2}$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Case A: } & (-3)^2 = (-3) \cdot (-3) = \mathbf{+9} \\[0.5em]
& \text{Parentheses explicitly include the negative sign inside the base being squared.} \\[1em]
\text{Case B: } & -3^2 = -(3^2) = -(3 \cdot 3) = \mathbf{-9} \\[0.5em]
& \text{Without parentheses, the exponent } 2 \text{ applies ONLY to the base } 3. \\
& \text{PEMDAS requires evaluating exponents BEFORE negation (multiplication by } -1).
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall:
**CRITICAL SMARTPHONE / CALCULATOR WARNING:**
- Typing $-3^2$ into Google or a smartphone calculator gives $-9$.
- To square negative 3, you MUST enter parentheses: $(-3)^2 = +9$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 8 covers what is arguably the single most common sign error in all of introductory algebra: the quantity negative 3 squared, versus negative 3 squared.

[TA Sora] Professor, countless points are lost on this on Exam 1! They look almost identical at first glance.

[Prof. Park] Let's train their eyes right now. Look at the first expression: open parenthesis, negative 3, close parenthesis, squared. Where is the negative sign, Sora?

[TA Sora] The negative sign is INSIDE the parentheses! The exponent 2 touches the parentheses, which means the entire quantity negative 3 is multiplied by itself: negative 3 times negative 3 gives positive 9!

[Prof. Park] Positive 9! Now look at the second expression: negative 3 squared without parentheses. What does the exponent touch here?

[TA Sora] It touches ONLY the 3! The minus sign is an outside negation waiting in front: negative of 3 squared, which is negative 9!

[Prof. Park] That is the crucial distinction: with parentheses, it is positive 9; without parentheses, it is negative 9. The base is only what the exponent directly touches!

[TA Sora] Unless parentheses wrap around the negative sign, that sign is not part of the base! Memorize this slide!
